newsitem.title: UK: British police win soccer trauma compensation.
newsitem.headline: British police win soccer trauma compensation.

text.p: Four British police officers who suffered severe mental trauma after attending to victims of the 1989 Hillsborough football disaster won compensation on Thursday.

Ninety-six fans were crushed to death at the Hillsborough soccer stadium during a match between English premier clubs Liverpool and Nottingham Forest when a crowd control barrier collapsed in an overcrowded seating area.

The Court of Appeal said they were exposed, by the admitted negligence of South Yorkshire police, to "excessively horrific events such as were likely to cause psychiatric illness even in a police officer".
The amount of damages they will receive has not been assessed pending a possible appeal to the House of Lords (upper house of parliament and England's highest appeal court).
The appeal judges overruled a earlier decision by a lower court that the police were not entitled to damages.
Actions brought by the four were seen as test cases for 17 other officers who dealt with injured and dying fans on the pitch and with bodies taken to mortuaries.
In April Britain's High Court rejected the action by the four officers saying they had not been placed beyond the normal call of duty.
Fourteen other policemen who carried out rescue work inside the spectator pens where many fans were crushed received a total of 1.2 million pounds ($1.9 million) damages from insurance companies.
Relatives of the 96 fans who died at Hillsborough, some of whom were refused stress damages while others received only modest sums, followed the appeal closely.
Trevor Hicks, who was at the stadium and lost daughters, Sarah, 19, and Victoria, 15, in the tragedy, said: "We are very disappointed.
"Obviously we have sympathy with the officers concerned but we think this is a bad decision." ($1=.6141 Pound)
